name: Carbohydrate loading

lead: Carbohydrate loading is a pre-event eating strategy that raises muscle and liver glycogen stores. Endurance athletes use it to delay fatigue, and physique competitors use a version of it so muscles look full.
Stored glycogen holds water, so loaded muscles can look rounder and fuller. A review found it postpones fatigue by roughly 20 percent in events over 90 minutes, with little effect on shorter efforts.

paras: In sport it is a high-carbohydrate pattern in the day or days before an event, often with reduced training. Bodybuilders use refeeds or a peak-week carb increase in the final days before a show.

Large carbohydrate meals can cause stomach upset and water-weight gain, and eating carbohydrate shortly before exercise can cause rebound low blood sugar in some people. Reviews describe dehydration and electrolyte manipulation before contests as potentially dangerous.

chain: Higher carbohydrate intake before a show
Muscles hold more water and look fuller
angle.text: Physique competitors raise carbohydrate in the final stage of prep so muscles look full on stage. The same strategy fuels long endurance events.

lead: Carbohydrate loading, or carb loading, is a dietary strategy that raises muscle and liver glycogen stores before an event. It was developed for endurance sport, where running out of glycogen coincides with exhaustion.[1][2]

For appearance, bodybuilders and physique athletes use a related approach in the final days of contest preparation. Because glycogen is stored with water, higher stores make muscles look fuller, a goal in peak-week planning.[3]

A sports medicine review reported that raising starting glycogen does not help short high-intensity efforts or 60-90 minute moderate events, but delays fatigue by about 20 percent in efforts beyond 90 minutes.[1]
infobox: About 2.7 g water per g carbohydrate (Wikipedia)

paras: Wikipedia describes carb loading as a pre-event approach for endurance athletes, beginning 36 to 48 hours before long events, with carbohydrate also consumed during and after.[2] Starchy, lower-fibre foods are commonly used, and athletes are advised to trial foods in training.[2]

A review of natural bodybuilding preparation covers carbohydrate intake in contest diets and warns that dehydration and electrolyte manipulation in the final days can be dangerous and may not improve appearance.[3]
Carbohydrate binds water, adding body weight, and large pre-event portions can cause digestive problems or insulin-related drops in blood sugar in susceptible people.[2]

A 1997 review found little benefit for short or moderate events and about a 20 percent delay in fatigue in efforts over 90 minutes, with some 2 to 3 percent performance gains in time trials.[1] A 2017 review covers post-exercise glycogen resynthesis.[4] Studies of preoperative carbohydrate loading exist in surgery but concern a different purpose.
